Inside: The invitation.
You take The invitation.
You put The invitation in raincoat.

Rain writes over the taxi's tyre marks. Velvet's side entrance glows beneath a narrow awning. The loading bay runs behind the building; a soup kiosk stays lit across the road.

You can see side door.

Exits: inside · loading bay · kiosk · home · front door.

Warm air. Wet wool. A corridor the colour of dried wine. A notice points left to the working toilets. The bar is ahead; a cloakroom opens on the right.

Here: Inez Vale.

A folded towel protects the counter. Two pencils wait beside mismatched cups. The main floor opens toward a small stage; stairs rise beside a quieter salon. A service door leads to the kitchen.

Here: Mara Venn.

You can see bar counter.

Exits: vestibule · outside · upstairs · kitchen · stage · salon · archive.
Don’t put your phone down there. It’s wet underneath the mat.
passages.speaker: mara

passages.text: You keep hold of it while she reads the invitation. She does not ask to touch the screen. For a moment she seems about to say something she has already rehearsed. Then an order comes in and she writes it on her wrist instead.
There’s a ledger going upstairs tonight. Tenant relief fund. Dates, amounts. Names.
passages.speaker: mara

passages.text: She puts a plate over a chipped mug and carries on speaking.
People got help after the flood. Some didn’t use the names they use now. I don’t want those names traded with the debt.
passages.speaker: mara

passages.text: You ask who would do that.
Someone who thinks a file is less messy than a person. Look, I used to keep the file. I’m not pretending I was better.
passages.speaker: mara

passages.speaker: mara

passages.text: You wait 40 minutes. The city keeps its own appointments.
Mara leaves to get on with the night.

The lamp is still on. The service table holds whatever you have left there.

You can see service envelope, The original ledger.

Exits: bar.
You open service envelope.
Inside: Carbon impression.
A maintenance queue receipt. M. VENN signed the override at 22:16.
Inside the envelope, the routing record matches the reference number on your invitation. The apartment signature was reused; it was never evidence that you had agreed to be here.

A carbon impression carries Mara’s handwriting and the maintenance-queue override: M. VENN / 22:16. She scheduled the invitation a minute before the printer ran. She knew the old machine would produce an independent paper trail.
The name on the authenticated record is Mara Venn.
She needed an independent witness outside the old tenant group.
You read it a second time, looking for something that would make the sender less responsible for your being here. The signature stays the same.
An explanation is a useful thing. It is not an apology.
You take The original ledger.
Your words are remembered. There is more to follow up in Velvet / the bar.

A folded towel protects the counter. Two pencils wait beside mismatched cups. The main floor opens toward a small stage; stairs rise beside a quieter salon. A service door leads to the kitchen.

You can see bar counter.

Exits: vestibule · outside · upstairs · kitchen · stage · salon · archive.
Redaction takes longer than you expected. Marker is not enough; held to a light, the names show through. Mara finds scissors. You cut copies, cover the gaps with clean paper, and copy the copies.
Luca checks the dates left visible. Twice he asks for one to stay. Twice you ask whether it identifies someone. Once he agrees to remove it. The other time you remove it anyway.
You do. Understanding a cost does not make it stop costing.
The originals go into separate sealed envelopes held by the people responsible for the fund. You keep the redacted copy and the routing proof. Evidence without a ready-made public spectacle.
Outside the office, the board representative is calling a taxi. They have acquired time. You have made that trade deliberately.

Rain writes over the taxi's tyre marks. Velvet's side entrance glows beneath a narrow awning. The loading bay runs behind the building; a soup kiosk stays lit across the road.

You can see side door.

Exits: inside · loading bay · kiosk · home · front door.

The refrigerator hums in two keys at once. Your mug is in the sink. The kettle waits beside an unclaimed patch of counter.

You can see kettle.

Exits: street · motel 27.
A flat envelope lies under the takeaway menus. Inside is a key tagged MOTEL 27, room 06, wrapped in a bus timetable. Inez has written her number beneath it.
Dawn finds the apartment before you have slept. The window turns from black to an unhelpful grey. Somewhere in the building, a shower starts.
The redacted accounts have reached the Static. The board has seven days to respond, and seven days to prepare. Mara is calling people one at a time for permission to corroborate.
You know who sent the invitation: Mara Venn. What remains uncertain is whether they have understood why the method mattered.
You preserved the accounts and protected the names. The people who can corroborate the ledger now get to decide whether they will. That is slower than a leak. The board is making use of every hour.
Mara sends a list of times when she is free to talk. Luca sends a list of gaps in the evidence. Neither is a thank-you note. Both assume you are still involved.
The original invitation sits beneath your redacted copy. You arrived as someone else’s unasked-for witness. You leave having made the next invitation conditional on an answer.
Elsewhere, a meeting you will never see begins with a person asking whether their name has to be written down. This time, the answer is no.

He means the upload. You think of every smaller chance that led here. Then the progress bar finishes.
The first response is a question about an amount. The second names a tenant. The third asks why someone’s address is different from the one in the file.
Mara stands in the door. She does not look at the phone.
Luca has stopped smiling at the upload. He starts writing a removal policy into a blank note. It is late to begin, but he begins.
The board announces an emergency meeting before you reach the stairs. Something has moved. So have the consequences.

passages.speaker: mara

Someone who thinks a file is less messy than a person. Look, I used to keep the file. I’m not pretending I was better.
passages.speaker: mara

Luca finds a working charger in the office. The battery icon appears with ridiculous cheer. He photographs each page against the dark desk.
He means the upload. You think of every smaller chance that led here. Then the progress bar finishes.
The first response is a question about an amount. The second names a tenant. The third asks why someone’s address is different from the one in the file.
Mara stands in the door. She does not look at the phone.
Luca has stopped smiling at the upload. He starts writing a removal policy into a blank note. It is late to begin, but he begins.
The board announces an emergency meeting before you reach the stairs. Something has moved. So have the consequences.

Dawn finds the apartment before you have slept. The window turns from black to an unhelpful grey. Somewhere in the building, a shower starts.
The complete ledger is public. An emergency board meeting is scheduled. Two tenants have asked to have their names removed from copies that can no longer be recalled.
You know who sent the invitation: Celeste Ardent. What remains uncertain is whether they have understood why the method mattered.
You made the original public. The board cannot quietly describe the transfer as routine. The fund is under scrutiny, and its members are answering questions they avoided for years.
People named in the ledger are answering questions too. Mara stops responding after her first message. Luca’s broadcast begins with a correction and a request not to contact the tenants.
You have changed the night for people who were not there. Some needed the change. Some did not consent to your version of it.
Your alias appears in the credits of the archive. Beneath it, a stranger has added a comment: “Who is this person?”

The original ledger goes into a lockbox. A second upstairs pass goes into your pocket. One object is much lighter than the other.

You traded custody for access. The agreement is real. So is the board’s use of it: an independent witness has entered a constructive relationship with the institution.

The original ledger is under your table, wrapped in a dry bag. The board proceeds with its own copy. Luca has begun looking for another source. Custody has given you responsibility without stopping the city.
You know who sent the invitation: Celeste Ardent. What remains uncertain is whether they have understood why the method mattered.
You kept the paper and declined the available alliances. Nobody gets to call your silence consent without an objection from you. Nobody has the original evidence to use against that claim either.

Your phone is quiet. In the next apartment, someone picks up a delivery at the door. You hear the driver ask for a signature.
